subject: English
central_question: How can a student change the grammatical form of a sentence while preserving its original meaning and logical relationship?
in_scope_units: Combining simple sentences into complex sentences using clauses
Combining simple sentences into compound sentences using coordinating conjunctions
Reducing a complex sentence to a simple sentence with a phrase
Transforming degrees of comparison without changing meaning
Transforming assertive sentences into interrogative or exclamatory forms

known_pitfalls.claim: Any conjunction can be used when combining sentences.
known_pitfalls.correction: The conjunction or clause marker must preserve the original logical relationship, such as reason, contrast, choice, or result.

known_pitfalls.claim: A clause can be reduced to any phrase as long as the sentence is shorter.
known_pitfalls.correction: The reduced phrase must preserve the same subject relationship and logical meaning as the original clause.

known_pitfalls.claim: Ravi is taller than any boy in the class is the exact comparative form of the superlative.
known_pitfalls.correction: The standard form is 'Ravi is taller than any other boy in the class.'

recommended_example_progression: Combine two simple sentences using an adverb clause of reason
Combine two simple sentences with a coordinating conjunction
Reduce a contrast clause to an in spite of phrase
Transform positive degree into comparative and superlative
Transform an assertive sentence into an exclamatory sentence
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: Typical CBSE practice includes sentence combining, rewriting without changing meaning, degree transformation, and assertive-interrogative-exclamatory conversion.
